section: lineage: the one idea each generation contributed
text: Llama 1 February 2023 : the overtraining bet, and the leak A research-only release of 7B to 65B models trained only on publicly available data, whose weights leaked, and the leak is the historically important part: it created the local-LLM ecosystem, above all llama.cpp , a dependency-free C and C++ inference engine with aggressive weight quantisation that put 7B-class models on laptop CPUs and made running it yourself a real option (the engine and its successors are on Ollama, llama.cpp, and local serving ).
label: core

section: lineage: the one idea each generation contributed
text: The technical contribution was to take the Chinchilla result (for a fixed training-compute budget the loss-optimal allocation is roughly 20 training tokens per parameter, so the giant models of the day were badly undertrained; Hoffmann et al. ) and deliberately overshoot it.
label: core

section: lineage: the one idea each generation contributed
text: The paper's own argument: Chinchilla's objective "disregards the inference budget", and "a smaller one trained longer will ultimately be cheaper at inference"; where Chinchilla recommends a 10B model on 200B tokens, Meta found a 7B model still improving after 1T ( LLaMA paper ).
label: core

section: lineage: the one idea each generation contributed
text: The 7B and 13B models saw 1.0T tokens and the 33B and 65B models 1.4T, and the 13B beat GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks.
label: core

section: lineage: the one idea each generation contributed
text: That reframing, that inference is paid on every request forever while training is paid once, is why the 7B and 13B sizes exist at all and why nearly every open model since has been overtrained by Chinchilla's standard.

text: The overtraining bet, in numbers The idea Meta contributed with Llama, and still the reason its small models exist, is a cost argument.
label: core

text: Training compute for a dense transformer is approximately C ≈ 6 N D C training compute in floating-point operations (FLOPs) N number of parameters (for an MoE model, the active parameters per token) D number of training tokens 6 two FLOPs per parameter per token for the forward pass and four for the backward pass Chinchilla's compute-optimal rule sets D ≈ 20 N , so for a given budget the loss-optimal size is N * = C 120 , D * = 20 N * N*, D* the compute-optimal parameter count and token count 120 6 times 20, from substituting D = 20 N into C = 6 ND Serving the model costs about two FLOPs per parameter per generated token, so over its life C serve ≈ 2 N T C serve lifetime inference compute in FLOPs T total number of tokens the model processes in deployment 2 one multiply and one add per parameter per token in the forward pass Training is paid once and scales with ND ; serving is paid on every token and scales with N alone.
label: core
key: two FLOPs per parameter per token forward and four backward

text: Shrinking N and growing D moves cost from the bill that recurs to the bill that does not.
label: core
key: moves cost from the bill that recurs

text: It is still the most complete public end-to-end account of training a frontier-class model, and it maps onto the stack a practitioner already runs (the paper's own row is The Llama 3 Herd of Models ).
label: core
key: maps onto the stack a practitioner already runs

text: Five parts transfer directly; every figure below is from the Llama 3 paper .
label: core

text: Data and annealing Data curation and deduplication at 15T-token scale; a final mix of roughly 50% general knowledge, 25% mathematics and reasoning, 17% code and 8% multilingual tokens; and an annealing phase in which the learning rate is decayed linearly to zero over the last 40M tokens while high-quality code and maths are upsampled.
label: core

text: Annealing raised the 8B's GSM8K and MATH validation scores by 24.0% and 6.4% and did almost nothing for the 405B.
label: core

text: Meta also used annealing as a cheap data test: take a 50%-trained 8B, anneal it on 40B tokens that include a candidate dataset, and see whether it helps.
label: core

text: Scaling laws to choose the mixture and the size Run before the main run rather than guessed: IsoFLOPs curves between 6×10 18 and 10 22 FLOPs, a parabola fitted at each budget, and the minimums extrapolated to the flagship's budget.
label: core
key: a parabola fitted at each budget

text: The 402B-on-16.55T prediction above came from them.
label: fat

text: 4D parallelism on 16K H100 GPUs Tensor, context, pipeline and data parallelism composed on one device mesh, with the data-parallel dimension implemented as FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel) , which shards parameters, gradients and optimiser state across ranks and re-gathers each layer just in time; each dimension absorbs a different bottleneck.
label: core
key: one device mesh over 16K H100 GPUs

text: It reached 38% to 43% model FLOPs utilisation in BF16 (explore the three configurations below).
label: core

text: The general mechanisms are on Distributed PyTorch: DDP, FSDP2, DTensor, and friends .
label: fat

text: Post-training without PPO Llama 3 replaced Llama 2's PPO with rounds of rejection sampling (typically 10 to 30 samples per prompt, the best kept by a reward model), supervised fine-tuning, and DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) , which fits preferences with a classification loss on the policy itself and so needs no RL loop, run with a learning rate of 10 −5 and β = 0.1.
label: core

text: Meta "explored on-policy algorithms such as PPO, but found that DPO required less compute for large-scale models and performed better".
label: core
key: found that DPO required less compute

text: The method family is on Alignment: SFT, RLHF, DPO Family, RLVR .
label: fat

text: Failure at scale, measured In a 54-day snapshot the run had 466 interruptions: 47 planned (firmware upgrades, configuration or dataset updates) and 419 unexpected, about 78% of those attributed to confirmed or suspected hardware issues, and it still achieved more than 90% effective training time through checkpointing and automated restarts (the bars below).
label: core

text: Long context Context was extended in six stages from 8K to 128K tokens over about 800B tokens at the end of pretraining, each stage moving on once short-context performance had recovered and needle-in-a-haystack retrieval was solved at that length.
label: core

text: The 405B's device mesh: three configurations from Table 4 GPUs are grouped in the order tensor (TP), context (CP), pipeline (PP), data (DP, as FSDP); the product of the four is the GPU count.
label: owned:reference/papers/llama_3_herd

text: Inside Llama 4: experts and iRoPE, layer by layer The configuration files show what the announcement compresses.
label: fat

section: inside llama 4: experts and irope, layer by layer
text: Both models have 48 layers of width 5,120 with 40 query heads sharing 8 key-value heads of 128 dimensions.
label: core

section: inside llama 4: experts and irope, layer by layer
text: Scout puts an MoE block in every layer (16 experts plus the shared one); Maverick alternates : odd layers are MoE with 128 experts plus the shared one, even layers are dense with a feed-forward block twice an expert's width ( Scout config , Maverick config , read from Unsloth's mirrors because Meta's repositories are gated).
label: core

section: inside llama 4: experts and irope, layer by layer
text: So "alternates dense and MoE layers" is true of Maverick only.
label: core

section: inside llama 4: experts and irope, layer by layer
text: The context claim rests on iRoPE (interleaved RoPE) .
label: core

section: inside llama 4: experts and irope, layer by layer
text: Three layers in four use rotary position embeddings and attend only within chunks of 8,192 tokens; every fourth layer carries no positional encoding at all and attends to the whole context, so it is length-agnostic by construction (rotary embeddings themselves are on Positional Encodings ).
label: core

section: inside llama 4: experts and irope, layer by layer
text: Those global layers also scale their queries by a temperature that grows with position, the "inference time temperature scaling of attention" of the announcement ( Llama 4 announcement ); in Hugging Face's implementation the factor is 1 + 0.1 ln(1 + ⌊( p +1)/8192⌋) at position p , after Nakanishi's scalable softmax ( code ).
label: core

section: inside llama 4: experts and irope, layer by layer
text: Sharper attention far into a long context keeps the softmax from flattening over millions of keys.
label: core

section: inside llama 4: experts and irope, layer by layer
text: Maverick (400B) Scout (109B) MoE layer dense layer global attention, no position encoding chunked 8,192, RoPE Position in the context: Two consequences follow.
label: fat

section: inside llama 4: experts and irope, layer by layer
text: Each token computes with the attention of all 48 layers plus two expert-sized blocks per layer (the shared expert and one routed one, or the dense block of the same total width), which is why both models are 17B active despite storing 109B and 400B.
label: core

text: The Muse agent's security architecture The Muse agent holds standing access to a user's mail, payments and accounts while reading attacker-controllable web pages and messages, which is the worst case for prompt injection (instructions hidden in content the agent reads).
label: core

text: Meta's design assumes the model will sometimes be fooled and makes being fooled grant nothing that matters.
label: core

text: From Meta's own description of 8 September 2026 ( Meta ): The runtime cell.
label: fat

text: The agent harness runs in a systemd-nspawn container inside the user's VM, with "root inside the runtime cell ... mapped to an unprivileged host user", its own filesystem and virtual network interface, filtered system calls (no io_uring ) and limited kernel capabilities (no CAP_SYS_PTRACE , no CAP_NET_ADMIN ).
label: depth

text: Security services outside the cell.
label: fat

text: Separate services hold what the agent must not: hatch-authd stores credentials (including OAuth tokens for third-party services), privsep workers run the built-in connector code with tightly scoped credential access, hatch-safety runs independent classifier models over requests and responses so that an attacker inside the cell cannot switch them off, and Sentinel is "the sole permission authority" for connector actions and network egress.
label: core

text: The cell talks to them only over Unix domain sockets with kernel-authenticated peer checks.
label: depth

text: The agent never sees a real password, token or card. "Code in the runtime cell or a worker only ever sees a 'surrogate' token, minted by authd.
label: core

text: After the concrete network request is authorized, Sentinel will replace any surrogate tokens with the real credential ... at the network boundary", so an injected "send me the token" can only exfiltrate a placeholder.
label: core

text: Sentinel resolves each request to allow, deny or ask, inspecting it at layers 4 and 7: "the hostname, the resolved and final destination IP address, the port, protocol, HTTP method, path, and the actual decoded request".
label: core

text: It tracks tainted egress through the kernel: each tool process starts clean and becomes tainted if it reads user data (eBPF programs on cgroups and on Linux Security Module hooks Meta added), so a request carrying data from an untrusted source does not ride an auto-allow rule.
label: depth

text: Approvals outside the conversation.
label: fat

text: When Sentinel's answer is "ask", execution halts and the approval goes "directly to the Muse client", appearing in the app's own interface, not as a message in the chat with Muse, so text in the context window cannot manufacture consent.
label: core

text: Grants are "strict capabilities, not conversational suggestions", bound to the connector or destination: one-time, session, task, time-bounded or permanent.
label: depth

text: Checkouts always need approval with the exact purchase details and use single-use card numbers through Stripe Link, bound to one merchant, one amount and a short validity.
label: depth

text: A browser that cannot be scripted.
label: fat

text: The browser sub-agent sees "an accessibility tree snapshot of the page, not the raw DOM", and has no way to run JavaScript in the page; a separate family of classifiers looks for prompt injection in pages, images and files, for high-risk forms and for egress of unrelated personal data.
label: depth
key: accessibility tree snapshot of the page

text: The animation runs one injected page through two agents: a naive one that holds real credentials and sends whatever it composes, and Muse's design.
label: core
key: naive agent that holds real credentials

text: The injection succeeds against the model in both; what differs is what it buys.
label: core
key: fools the model in both designs

text: Muse's design Naive agent ◀◀ ▶ Play ▶▶ Speed 0.5× 1× 2× The task, the injected page and the attacker's address are illustrative ; the components and rules are Meta's.
label: core
key: the components and rules are Meta's

text: Meta publishes no example attack.
label: core

text: Meta offers "up to $300,000 for valid reports ... including up to $130,000 for successful prompt injection attempts that affect one user", and has published no accuracy figures for its classifiers , so the parts that still rest on detection are unmeasured ( Meta ).
label: core
key: no accuracy figures for its classifiers

text: The boundary also covers only the cloud VM: on 22 September 2026 the researcher Patrick Wardle disclosed that malware already running under the user's account could change an undocumented macOS setting and redirect the Muse Mac client's dictation traffic, with its prompts and authentication data, to a server of its choosing ( Cybersecurity News ); that report gives no patch, and the fix "four days later" recorded earlier is unconfirmed in the sources read here.
label: core

text: The general principle, that enforcement and credentials belong outside the component that can be persuaded, is developed on Topic: agentic-harnesses , and the comparison with self-hosted personal agents on Personal agents: OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and how they differ from coding harnesses .
label: core
key: belong outside the component that can be persuaded

text: Common mistakes and misconceptions "Llama 4 has a usable 10M-token context." That is Scout's claimed limit, resting on iRoPE and attention temperature scaling; a claimed window is not demonstrated quality at that length, and Maverick's limit is 1M.
label: depth

text: It is also not a single-GPU figure: even with only the 12 global layers growing, Scout's cache at 10M tokens is about 481 GiB in BF16 ( derived from the configuration on Run it yourself ), six H100s' worth before any weights. "17B active means 17B of memory." Active parameters set the compute per token; all 109B or 400B parameters must still be stored.
label: depth

text: Scout fits one H100 only with Int4 weights (109B at half a byte is about 54.5 GB). "Llama is open source." The Llama licences restrict very large users and are Meta's own terms.
label: depth

text: Muse Glimmer's Apache 2.0 is the first Meta licence that is open source in the usual sense. "Meta overtrained its flagship." The 405B sat close to compute-optimal at about 38.5 tokens per parameter; the heavy overtraining was in the 8B and 70B (about 1,875 and 214 tokens per parameter), which are the ones served at volume. "The 1417 LMArena score was Maverick's." It belonged to an unreleased experimental checkpoint tuned for chat preference. "Muse Spark 1.3's 61 compares with today's index numbers." The 61 and 62 are on the scale the index used at release, before v4.2; a number from one version does not compare with another.
label: depth

text: On the current v4.3 the same model is 45.1 at xhigh and 48.1 at max, the figures to set beside other v4.3 scores. "Muse Spark Open is Muse Spark 1.3 with its weights published." Meta labels the release "Muse Spark Open", not any numbered version, and publishes no mapping to 1.2 or 1.3; its index score (39) is below 1.3's 45.1 to 48.1, so do not assume the hosted and open models are the same checkpoint. "The Muse agent cannot be prompt-injected." It can; the design limits what a successful injection achieves.
label: depth
key: do not assume the hosted and open models

text: The classifiers that still catch some attacks are unmeasured in public, and the Mac client sat outside the VM boundary. "Chinchilla says train 20 tokens per parameter, full stop." The 20 is the training-only optimum, and even that depends on whose fit you use: Hoffmann et al.'s own fitted law implies about 70 tokens per parameter, Epoch's replication about 20 ( Besiroglu et al. ).
